clue.text: Paper got up by Hergesheimer

parts.note: a large sheet size of writing paper, plus 'got up' as a stand-in for 'rose', points to the American novelist Joseph Hergesheimer's 1934 novel whose title pairs that paper with Rose

explanation.surface: An American novelist runs off a batch of stationery.
explanation.walkthrough: Hergesheimer wrote The Foolscap Rose; 'got up' is a cryptic way of saying 'rose', so the paper that 'rose' in his title is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a traditional British paper size, about 13 by 16 inches, named after an old watermark of a jester's cap.

clue.text: French opera

parts.note: opera is the Latin plural of opus, so the clue asks for the French word for works, not for an operatic piece

explanation.surface: A request for a piece of Gallic musical drama.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Opera' looks like the musical form, but it is the plural of opus; the French plural for an artist's works is wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: The French plural noun for an artist's complete body of works, matching Latin opera as plural of opus.

clue.text: Gustafson's was not dry

parts.note: the Canadian poet Ralph Gustafson published a collection whose title pictures a scene with rain, so his was not dry

explanation.surface: Someone called Gustafson is complaining about the wet weather.
explanation.walkthrough: Ralph Gustafson's 1980 collection is Landscape with Rain, which won Canada's Governor General's Award; a view 'with rain' is not dry.
explanation.definitionFit: A painting or view of countryside scenery, here the one in Gustafson's book title that comes with rain.

clue.text: Descriptive of swift clinch, say

parts.note: swift reads as quick-witted and a clinch is an old word for a pun, so the clue asks for an adjective praising a nimble witticism

explanation.surface: A boxing commentator describes a fast grab in the ring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clinch' suggests boxing, but in older English it meant a pun or play on words; 'swift' hints at quickness of mind, perhaps also at Jonathan Swift.
explanation.definitionFit: Quick-witted and ingenious, the natural praise for a smart, fast pun.

clue.text: Pylon School member's drama settled bilaterally

definitions.meaning: the Pylon School was the 1930s group of poets around W H Auden, whose verse drama of 1928 carries this title
said of a bet or debt cleared by each party, money handed over by both camps

explanation.surface: A 1930s poet's play is described as having been agreed by both parties.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'Pylon School' (Auden, Spender, Day Lewis, MacNeice) was named after Spender's poem The Pylons; Auden's charade Paid on Both Sides was his early verse drama.
explanation.definitionFit: Auden's early verse play shares its title with a phrase for a payment made by each of two parties.

clue.text: Ira? Bob, perhaps? or Luca, the sculptor?

indicators.note: the question marks and 'perhaps' suggest these two names are only a possible version of the letters, inviting a reshuffle

explanation.surface: A guess at the identity of a man: an Ira, a Bob, or the Florentine artist Luca.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' tells you to rearrange IRA and BOB together; the six letters give the surname of the Renaissance sculptor Luca della Robbia.
explanation.definitionFit: Luca della Robbia was the fifteenth-century Florentine sculptor famed for glazed terracotta.

clue.text: The dialogue concerning Joe?

parts.note: re is a short word meaning about or concerning
Joe Public is the ordinary member of the public, so Joe stands for the second word

explanation.surface: Someone asks which conversation is about a man called Joe.
explanation.walkthrough: Joe Public is the British and American nickname for an ordinary person, so 'Joe' supplies PUBLIC.
explanation.definitionFit: Plato's most famous philosophical work is a dialogue on justice and the ideal state.

clue.text: Friend of 19 is bitter with new composition

indicators.note: composition means putting together, so the letters of these words are assembled into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A friend of a poet turns sour over his latest piece of music.
explanation.walkthrough: 'composition' signals rearranging BITTER into BRITTE, then N (new) follows. The composer Benjamin Britten collaborated with Auden, the answer to 19.
explanation.definitionFit: Benjamin Britten worked closely with Auden on songs, film scores and the opera Paul Bunyan.

clue.text: Gigantic size of book of maps?

definitions.meaning: huge, like the Titan Atlas who held up the heavens
an atlas is a book of maps, and the adjective from it can describe its large format

explanation.surface: Someone asks how big an enormous atlas is.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective from the Titan Atlas means huge and strong, and also suits the large format of a map book.

clue.text: Mechanical producer of Shakespeare

parts.note: in A Midsummer Night's Dream the rude mechanicals are Athenian workmen, and the carpenter among them stages their play

explanation.surface: Something that automatically turns out Shakespeare plays.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mechanical' suggests a machine, but in A Midsummer Night's Dream the 'mechanicals' are the tradesmen; Peter Quince directs their play of Pyramus and Thisbe.
explanation.definitionFit: Peter Quince, the carpenter, is the workman who organises and directs the amateur play within the comedy.

clue.text: Knight's theme

parts.note: the critic G Wilson Knight wrote a 1931 study of Shakespeare's Roman plays whose title names a theme of empire

explanation.surface: A chivalric knight's favourite subject.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Knight' looks like a mounted warrior, but it is the Shakespeare critic G. Wilson Knight, author of The Imperial Theme, itself a phrase from Macbeth.
explanation.definitionFit: Relating to an empire or emperor, the adjective in Wilson Knight's book title.

clue.text: He seems to thrive on nothing on a noisy island

definitions.text: He seems to thrive on nothing on a noisy island

indicators.note: in an across clue 'on' places the first piece before the next

parts.note: to thrive is to flourish or do well
O, the figure zero, stands for nothing

explanation.surface: A man somehow flourishes with nothing on a clamorous isle.
explanation.walkthrough: In The Tempest Caliban says 'the isle is full of noises'; the magician Prospero rules that island.
explanation.definitionFit: The deposed Duke of Milan, ruling an island in The Tempest, whose name itself suggests prospering.

clue.text: Isabella Mary offered thought for food

definitions.text: Isabella Mary offered thought for food

parts.words: Isabella Mary offered thought for food
parts.note: Isabella Mary was the Victorian author of the famous Book of Household Management, which gave readers ideas about cooking

explanation.surface: A woman named Isabella Mary gave people something to think about.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase twists 'food for thought'; Isabella Mary Beeton's 1861 Book of Household Management made her Britain's best-known cookery writer.
explanation.definitionFit: Mrs Beeton, born Isabella Mary Mayson, is the classic Victorian authority on cookery and housekeeping.

clue.text: "We all assume that -— said it" (Dorothy Parker)

definitions.text: "We all assume that -— said it" (Dorothy Parker)

parts.words: "We all assume that -— said it" (Dorothy Parker)
parts.note: Dorothy Parker's light verse on a famously witty Irish playwright says every bon mot gets credited to him

explanation.surface: A quotation from Dorothy Parker with a gap to fill.
explanation.walkthrough: Parker's poem on Oscar Wilde: 'If, with the literate, I am / Impelled to try an epigram, / I never seek to take the credit; / We all assume that Oscar said it.'
explanation.definitionFit: The first name of Wilde, the playwright so famous for epigrams that any clever quip is credited to him.

clue.text: C. Day Lewis worked these openings to death

definitions.text: C. Day Lewis worked these openings to death

parts.words: C. Day Lewis worked these openings to death
parts.note: Cecil Day Lewis published a 1938 poetry collection whose title couples musical openings with death

explanation.surface: A poet overused his favourite opening lines.
explanation.walkthrough: 'worked to death' suggests overuse, but Day Lewis's book is Overtures to Death; 'openings' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Orchestral introductions or opening approaches, as in Day Lewis's collection Overtures to Death.

clue.text: Niobe case re-examined in expression of respect

indicators.note: a case looked at again, reworked, signals rearranging the letters of the words before it

explanation.surface: The myth of Niobe is reconsidered by someone paying homage.
explanation.walkthrough: The signal word tells you to rearrange NIOBE and CASE, nine letters in all, while the surface reads as a fresh look at the myth.
explanation.definitionFit: A bow or curtsy is a gesture of deference or homage.

clue.text: Foolish knight also once adored

parts.note: in Twelfth Night the silly knight Sir Andrew says 'I was adored once too', echoing Sir Toby

explanation.surface: A daft knight recalls he too was loved in his time.
explanation.walkthrough: In Twelfth Night Sir Toby says Maria adores him, and Sir Andrew replies wistfully 'I was adored once too.'
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Andrew is the gullible, foolish knight of Twelfth Night.

clue.text: Star attraction in book

parts.note: an asterisk, a printed star, draws the reader's eye to an extra remark at the bottom of the page

explanation.surface: The headline turn in a show is described in a book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Star attraction' looks like a celebrity, but the star is an asterisk, which points the reader down the page.
explanation.definitionFit: A note printed at the foot of a page, often marked with an asterisk.

clue.text: Value on margin of Irish writer

indicators.note: in an across clue one piece set 'on' another follows it

parts.note: an edge is the margin or border of something
worth is value or merit

explanation.surface: An Irish author's worth is measured at the edges.
explanation.walkthrough: Maria Edgeworth (1768-1849) was the Anglo-Irish novelist of Castle Rackrent.
explanation.definitionFit: Maria Edgeworth, the Anglo-Irish novelist of Castle Rackrent.

clue.text: Sea-god said to be sea-green

indicators.note: said marks a word spoken, so this name matches the sound of another word

parts.note: glaucous means a pale bluish or sea green

explanation.surface: A god of the sea is reputed to be green like the waves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'said to be' signals a sound-alike: the adjective glaucous (sea-green) is pronounced like the god's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Glaucus was a Greek fisherman turned sea deity.

clue.text: Gold at lair of S's creator ()

indicators.note: at sets the two pieces side by side

parts.note: Au is the chemical symbol for gold
a den is a wild animal's lair

explanation.surface: Treasure in an animal's lair belongs to a creator.
explanation.walkthrough: 'S' is the OCR text for 5: the clue points to 5 down, Paid on Both Sides, the drama W H Auden wrote.
explanation.definitionFit: The poet who wrote the verse drama Paid on Both Sides, the answer at 5.

clue.text: Mrs Humphry Ward protagonist awarded victory by Mary Braddon

definitions.meaning: Mrs Humphry Ward wrote a 1900 novel named after its heroine
Mary Elizabeth Braddon wrote the 1863 novel whose title gives this woman a victory

explanation.surface: A heroine of one Victorian novelist wins a triumph from another.
explanation.walkthrough: Mrs Humphry Ward's novel is Eleanor (1900); M. E. Braddon's is Eleanor's Victory (1863).
explanation.definitionFit: A woman's first name that titles both a Humphry Ward novel and Braddon's Eleanor's Victory.

clue.text: Selkirk changed course

indicators.note: changed means altered, telling you the letters of the next word take a new order

explanation.surface: A Scotsman named Selkirk alters his route.
explanation.walkthrough: 'changed' signals rearranging COURSE. Alexander Selkirk, marooned on a Pacific island, inspired Defoe's castaway.
explanation.definitionFit: Alexander Selkirk, the real marooned sailor, was the model for Defoe's fictional castaway.

clue.text: Location of storm? or sleepy creature?

definitions.text: Location of storm? or sleepy creature?

parts.words: Location of storm? or sleepy creature?
parts.note: the American 'tempest in a' kitchen vessel, and the Mad Hatter's tea party where the drowsy Dormouse is stuffed into one

explanation.surface: Someone asks where a storm happened, or where an animal is sleeping.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'tempest in a teapot' is the US version of a storm in a teacup; in Alice's Adventures in Wonderland the Hatter and Hare push the sleepy Dormouse into the teapot.
explanation.definitionFit: The vessel for brewing tea, home of a proverbial storm and of Carroll's dozing Dormouse.

clue.text: He felt that discretion was not the better part of biography

definitions.text: He felt that discretion was not the better part of biography

parts.words: He felt that discretion was not the better part of biography
parts.note: plays on 'discretion is the better part of valour' for the author of Eminent Victorians, who made biography candid and irreverent

explanation.surface: A man thought tactfulness was not what makes a life story good.
explanation.walkthrough: Lytton Strachey wrote 'Discretion is not the better part of biography'; his Eminent Victorians debunked its subjects.
explanation.definitionFit: Lytton Strachey, the Bloomsbury biographer who wrote frankly irreverent lives of Victorian figures.

clue.text: Suburban provenance of a woman once in the right

definitions.text: Suburban provenance of a woman once in the right

parts.words: Suburban provenance of a woman once in the right
parts.note: the old song about a sweet lass from a hill in a London suburb on the Thames, a woman praised as being just right

explanation.surface: Where a woman who was once proved correct came from in the suburbs.
explanation.walkthrough: The 18th-century song 'The Lass of Richmond Hill' praises a girl from Richmond, a suburb of south-west London.
explanation.definitionFit: Richmond is a riverside suburb of south-west London, home of the lass in the old song.

clue.text: Humorous writer strikes severe note

parts.note: stern means severe or strict
E is one of the musical notes

explanation.surface: A comic author makes a grave remark.
explanation.walkthrough: Laurence Sterne wrote Tristram Shandy; 'strikes' is a link word, the writer hitting upon the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Laurence Sterne, author of the comic novel Tristram Shandy.

clue.text: Seed of opening phrase in children's story

definitions.meaning: the small oily seed of a plant used in baking
in Ali Baba and the Forty Thieves the cave opens at the command 'Open' followed by this word

explanation.surface: Where a seed comes from: the opening words of a fairy tale.
explanation.definitionFit: The password in Ali Baba that opens the robbers' cave, and also a common edible seed.

clue.text: Orators who hit top form after a second

indicators.note: after puts the people who reach a peak behind the short piece

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for a second of time
those who peak reach their highest point, so they are peakers

explanation.surface: Public speakers hit their best form after a moment's pause.
explanation.walkthrough: S (second) is followed by PEAKERS, those who peak or reach top form.
explanation.definitionFit: People who give speeches in public.
